title: Trigonometric Identities
learningObjective: Use the sum and difference, the double-angle, and power-reducing formulas for cosine, sine, and tangent and the Pythagorean identities.

faqs.question: What is a trigonometric identity, and how is it different from an equation?
Where do the three Pythagorean identities come from?
faqs.answer:
A point on the unit circle at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ) (TR5). The right triangle it forms has legs cos θ and sin θ and a hypotenuse of 1, so the Pythagorean Theorem gives the first identity. Divide every term by cos²θ or by sin²θ and you get the other two.

A point on the unit circle at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), and it forms a right triangle with hypotenuse 1. The Pythagorean Theorem then gives the first Pythagorean identity.

Deriving all three

\( \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 \)

Divide by \( \cos^2\theta \): \( \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} + 1 = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} \) → \( \tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta \)

Divide by \( \sin^2\theta \): \( 1 + \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \) → \( 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta \)

Each one can be rearranged too: \( \cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta \) and \( \sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta \).

faqs.question: Why isn't sin(A + B) just sin A + sin B?
faqs.answer:
Because sine is a function, not a number you can distribute over a sum. One counterexample is enough to show it: \( \sin\!\left(\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\!\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1 \), but \( \sin\pi + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0 + 1 = 1 \). The same is true for cosine and tangent. There is a correct rule for the sine of a sum, but it has more pieces (faq-4).

Adding the angles first (π + π/2 = 3π/2) lands somewhere completely different than adding the two sine values. The same is true for cosine and tangent.

faqs.question: Where do the sum and difference formulas come from?
faqs.answer:
Put two points on the unit circle, one at angle \( \alpha \) and one at angle \( \beta \). Rotate the picture clockwise by \( \beta \) so the second point lands on \( (1, 0) \). Rotating doesn't change the distance between the points, so computing that distance both ways with the distance formula and setting the results equal gives \( \cos(\alpha-\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta \). The other five formulas follow the same way.

The chord between two points on the unit circle has the same length before and after rotating the picture. Finding that length with the distance formula both ways, then setting them equal, gives cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β.

The six formulas

\( \sin(\alpha+\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta \)

\( \sin(\alpha-\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta \)

\( \cos(\alpha+\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta \)

\( \cos(\alpha-\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta \)

\( \tan(\alpha+\beta) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta} \)

\( \tan(\alpha-\beta) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha-\tan\beta}{1+\tan\alpha\tan\beta} \)

Memory tip: the sine formulas keep the sign (a plus in \( \sin(\alpha+\beta) \)), while the cosine formulas flip it (a minus in \( \cos(\alpha+\beta) \)).

faqs.question: How are the double-angle formulas related to the sum formulas?
faqs.answer:
A double angle is just an angle added to itself. Set \( \alpha = \beta \) in each sum formula and simplify.
Setting α = β

\( \sin(\alpha+\alpha) = \sin\alpha\cos\alpha + \cos\alpha\sin\alpha \;\Rightarrow\; \sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha \)

\( \cos(\alpha+\alpha) = \cos\alpha\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha\sin\alpha \;\Rightarrow\; \cos 2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha \)

\( \tan(\alpha+\alpha) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha+\tan\alpha}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\alpha} \;\Rightarrow\; \tan 2\alpha = \dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha} \)

faqs.question: How are the power-reducing and half-angle formulas related to the double-angle formulas?
faqs.answer:
Solve two of the forms of \( \cos 2\theta \) for \( \sin^2\theta \) and \( \cos^2\theta \) and you have the power-reducing formulas. Replace \( \theta \) with \( \tfrac{\theta}{2} \) in those and you have the half-angle formulas. So you only need to remember the parents; the rest can be rebuilt.

The whole section is one family: the sum formulas are the parents, and each later formula comes from the one before it. Remember the parents and you can rebuild the rest.

Rebuilding them

\( \cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \;\Rightarrow\; \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1-\cos 2\theta}{2} \)

\( \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2} \)

\( \tan^2\theta = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{1-\cos 2\theta}{1+\cos 2\theta} \)

Replace \( \theta \) with \( \tfrac{\theta}{2} \): \( \sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; \sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{2}} \)

faqs.question: How do I use a Pythagorean identity to find the other trig values when I'm given one (and get the sign right)?
faqs.answer:
Use the identity to solve for the square of the missing function, take the square root, and let the quadrant choose the sign. Then get everything else from quotients and reciprocals.
Worked Example

Given \( \cos\theta = -\dfrac{3}{5} \) with \( \theta \) in Quadrant II.

\( \sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = 1 - \dfrac{9}{25} = \dfrac{16}{25} \), so \( \sin\theta = \pm\dfrac{4}{5} \). Sine is positive in Quadrant II, so \( \sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5} \).

\( \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{4/5}{-3/5} = -\dfrac{4}{3} \), and the reciprocals are \( \csc\theta = \dfrac{5}{4} \), \( \sec\theta = -\dfrac{5}{3} \), \( \cot\theta = -\dfrac{3}{4} \).

faqs.question: Why does cos(2θ) have three forms, and how do I pick one?
faqs.answer:
All three are the same value. Start with \( \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta \). Replacing \( \cos^2\theta \) with \( 1-\sin^2\theta \) (a Pythagorean identity) gives \( 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \), and replacing \( \sin^2\theta \) with \( 1-\cos^2\theta \) gives \( 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \). Pick the form that uses only the function you already know.
Choosing a form

Know only \( \sin\theta \)? Use \( \cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \).

Know only \( \cos\theta \)? Use \( \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \).

Know both? Use \( \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta \).

Example: if \( \sin\alpha = \dfrac{2}{3} \), then \( \cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{8}{9} = \dfrac{1}{9} \).

faqs.question: How do I use the sum and difference formulas to find an exact value like cos 75°?
faqs.answer:
Split the angle into a sum or difference of two special angles, write the matching formula, substitute the unit-circle values, and simplify.

To find an exact value at 75°, split it into two angles whose sine and cosine you already know — here 30° and 45° — then use the sum formula.

Worked Example

\( 75° = 30° + 45° \)

\( \cos 75° = \cos(30°+45°) = \cos 30°\cos 45° - \sin 30°\sin 45° \)

\( = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4} \)

Check with a calculator: \( \dfrac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4} \approx 0.2588 \) and \( \cos 75° \approx 0.2588 \).

faqs.question: How do I spot a sum or difference formula "running backward" (like cos 87° cos 33° − sin 87° sin 33°)?
faqs.answer:
Look for products of two cosines, or of a sine and a cosine, joined by a plus or minus. The pattern tells you which formula was expanded: \( \cos\cos - \sin\sin \) is \( \cos(\text{sum}) \); \( \cos\cos + \sin\sin \) is \( \cos(\text{difference}) \); \( \sin\cos + \cos\sin \) is \( \sin(\text{sum}) \); \( \sin\cos - \cos\sin \) is \( \sin(\text{difference}) \). Collapse it back into one function of one angle.
Worked Examples

\( \cos 87°\cos 33° - \sin 87°\sin 33° = \cos(87°+33°) = \cos 120° = -\dfrac{1}{2} \)

\( \sin 20°\cos 80° - \cos 20°\sin 80° = \sin(20°-80°) = \sin(-60°) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \)

\( \dfrac{\tan 40° - \tan 10°}{1 + \tan 40°\tan 10°} = \tan(40°-10°) = \tan 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \)

Order matters in a difference: in the second example, \( \sin 20° \) comes first, so the angle is \( 20° - 80° \), not \( 80° - 20° \).

faqs.question: Given sin α and its quadrant, how do I find sin 2α, cos 2α, and tan 2α?
faqs.answer:
First find cos α with a Pythagorean identity (the quadrant gives the sign), then substitute both values into the double-angle formulas.
Worked Example

Given \( \sin\alpha = \dfrac{2}{3} \) with \( \alpha \) in Quadrant I.

\( \cos^2\alpha = 1 - \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{5}{9} \), and cosine is positive in Quadrant I, so \( \cos\alpha = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \).

\( \sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = 2\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{9} \)

\( \cos 2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha = \dfrac{5}{9} - \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{1}{9} \)

\( \tan 2\alpha = \dfrac{\sin 2\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}/9}{1/9} = 4\sqrt{5} \)

faqs.question: How do I use power-reducing formulas to rewrite something like sin⁴β without powers?
faqs.answer:
Write the power as a square of a square, replace the inner square with its power-reducing formula, expand, and reduce again. The second time, the angle doubles, so \( 2\beta \) becomes \( 4\beta \).
Worked Example

\( \sin^4\beta = (\sin^2\beta)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1-\cos 2\beta}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2\beta + \cos^2 2\beta}{4} \)

Reduce the leftover square: \( \cos^2 2\beta = \dfrac{1+\cos 4\beta}{2} \)

\( \sin^4\beta = \dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2\beta + \frac{1+\cos 4\beta}{2}}{4} = \dfrac{3 - 4\cos 2\beta + \cos 4\beta}{8} \)

Quick check at \( \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \): the left side is \( 1 \), and the right side is \( \dfrac{3 + 4 + 1}{8} = 1 \).

faqs.question: How do I use a half-angle formula to find an exact value like sin 15°?
faqs.answer:
Ask what your angle is half of, choose the formula and its sign, substitute, and simplify. For 15°, that's half of 30°, and 15° is in Quadrant I, so sine is positive.

To use a half-angle formula for 15°, ask "15° is half of what?" — it's half of 30°, so θ = 30° goes into the formula.

Worked Example

\( \sin 15° = \sin\dfrac{30°}{2} = +\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos 30°}{2}} \)

\( = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2-\sqrt{3}}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{3}}}{2} \)

Check: \( \dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{3}}}{2} \approx 0.2588 \). The difference formula gives the same number in another form: \( \sin 15° = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4} \approx 0.2588 \).

faqs.question: How do I choose the + or − in a half-angle formula, and is there a form that avoids it?
faqs.answer:
The \( \pm \) isn't asking you to use both. Pick one sign using the quadrant of the half angle \( \tfrac{\theta}{2} \), not the quadrant of \( \theta \). For tangent you can skip the sign entirely: \( \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} \).

Signs of sine, cosine, and tangent by quadrant. For a half-angle formula, use the quadrant that the half angle θ/2 lands in (here 165°, Quadrant II).

Worked Examples

\( \cos 75° = \cos\dfrac{150°}{2} \). Quadrant I, so cosine is positive: \( \sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos 150°}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{3}}}{2} \approx 0.2588 \)

\( \sin 165° = \sin\dfrac{330°}{2} \). Quadrant II, so sine is positive: \( \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos 330°}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{3}}}{2} \)

\( \tan 15° = \dfrac{\sin 30°}{1+\cos 30°} = \dfrac{1/2}{1+\sqrt{3}/2} = 2-\sqrt{3} \) (no sign to choose)

faqs.question: How do I decide which formula to reach for?
faqs.answer:
Match what you see in the problem to the family that fits it. If more than one formula could work, choose the one that only needs values you already know.

A quick chooser: match what you see in the problem to the formula family that fits it.

faqs.question: How do these formulas extend the exact values from the unit circle and reference angles (TR5)?
faqs.answer:
TR5 gave exact values only at multiples of 30° and 45°. Combining those with the sum, difference, double-angle, and half-angle formulas reaches many more, like 15°, 75°, 105°, and 165°, and their reference-angle relatives in every quadrant (for example, sin 165° uses the reference angle 15°).

TR5 gave exact values only at multiples of 30° and 45° (gray). Sum, difference, double-, and half-angle formulas reach angles like 15° and 75° (orange).

faqs.question: How does this section set up TE2 (verifying identities) and TE3 (solving equations)?
faqs.answer: TE2 asks you to prove that two expressions are equal, using these formulas as your toolkit — knowing the forms of \( \cos 2\theta \) (faq-8) and the Pythagorean identities (faq-2) is what lets you choose a path. TE3 uses the same formulas to rewrite an equation so it can be solved, for example turning \( \sin 2x \) into \( 2\sin x\cos x \) so you can factor.

faqs.question: Why do these identities matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: In calculus, the sum formula is used to work out the derivative of sine, and the power-reducing formulas are what make integrals like \( \int \sin^2 x \, dx \) doable. In physics and engineering, these formulas describe how waves combine — sound, light, and alternating current — including interference and beats.

guided.title: Practice Deriving the Pythagorean Identities
guided.prompt: I'm learning where the Pythagorean identities come from. Ask me to start with a point on the unit circle and explain why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Then guide me step by step to derive 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ by dividing, asking me what to divide by and why. Check my reasoning at each step.

guided.title: Practice Exact Values with Sum and Difference Formulas
guided.prompt: I'm learning to find exact values like cos 75° or sin 15° with the sum and difference formulas. Give me an angle, ask me how to split it into two special angles, and coach me through substituting and simplifying without giving the answer up front. Then give me two more angles (one in radians) and check my work.

guided.title: Practice Spotting a Formula Running Backward
guided.prompt: Give me several expressions like cos 87° cos 33° − sin 87° sin 33° or sin 20° cos 80° − cos 20° sin 80°. For each one, ask me which sum or difference formula it matches before I simplify, and check my answer. Include one tangent example.

guided.title: Practice Double-Angle and Half-Angle Problems
guided.prompt: Give me a problem where I'm told sin α and the quadrant of α, and ask me to find sin 2α, cos 2α, and tan 2α, walking me through finding cos α first. Then give me a half-angle problem like sin 15° or cos 75°, and ask me to justify the sign using the quadrant of the half angle.

guided.title: Connect All the Formulas as One Family
guided.prompt: I want to understand how the sum, double-angle, power-reducing, and half-angle formulas are related instead of memorizing each one. Walk me through deriving each from the one before it, asking me to do the key step each time (setting α = β, solving for sin²θ, replacing θ with θ/2). Then quiz me on which formula I would use in a few situations.

stages.desc: Three quick reviews TE1 leans on: unit-circle values and signs (TR5), splitting angles with common denominators, and radical arithmetic. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Unit-circle values and quadrant signs
stops.target: Know \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) of \(\tfrac{\pi}{6},\tfrac{\pi}{4},\tfrac{\pi}{3}\), and use reference angles and quadrant signs for other special angles (TR5).
stops.coldPlain: Find the exact value: (1) sin(5pi/6) (2) cos(5pi/4) (3) sin(-pi/3)
stops.solution: (1) Reference angle pi/6, Quadrant II, sine positive: 1/2. (2) Reference angle pi/4, Quadrant III, cosine negative: -sqrt(2)/2. (3) Reference angle pi/3, Quadrant IV, sine negative: -sqrt(3)/2.
stops.mistake: Mixing up which of sqrt(3)/2 and 1/2 goes with pi/6 versus pi/3.
stops.reflect: Every exact value in TE1 is built from these few numbers. Which one do you mix up most?

stops.title: Split an angle into special angles
stops.target: Rewrite an angle like \(\tfrac{7\pi}{12}\) as a sum or difference of special angles using a common denominator, and spot when an angle is half of a special angle.
stops.cold: (1) Write \(\tfrac{7\pi}{12}\) as a sum of two special angles. (2) Write \(\tfrac{\pi}{12}\) as a difference. (3) \(\tfrac{\pi}{8}\) is half of which special angle?
stops.coldPlain: (1) Write 7pi/12 as a sum of two special angles. (2) Write pi/12 as a difference. (3) pi/8 is half of which special angle?
stops.solution: Twelfths: pi/6 = 2pi/12, pi/4 = 3pi/12, pi/3 = 4pi/12. So 7pi/12 = 4pi/12 + 3pi/12 = pi/3 + pi/4 and pi/12 = pi/3 - pi/4. pi/8 is half of pi/4 (= 2pi/8).
stops.mistake: Splitting 7pi/12 into 7pi/6 and pi/2 by adding numerators and denominators separately.
stops.again: (1) \(\tfrac{11\pi}{12}\) as a sum (2) \(\tfrac{5\pi}{8}\) is half of what?
stops.reflect: Why is twelfths the right common denominator for pi/6, pi/4, and pi/3?

stops.title: Arithmetic with radicals
stops.target: Multiply and combine fractions with radicals, and simplify a fraction inside a square root.
stops.coldA: (1) \(\tfrac{\sqrt6}{4}-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\) (2) Multiply top and bottom of the inner fraction by 2: \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2}\)
stops.solution: (1) sqrt3 times sqrt2 is sqrt6, 2 times 2 is 4; same denominator so combine: (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4. (2) Multiply the inner fraction by 2/2 to clear the small fraction: (2 - sqrt3)/4, then sqrt of 4 is 2: sqrt(2 - sqrt3)/2.
stops.mistake: Writing sqrt6 - sqrt2 as sqrt4; you cannot combine different radicals by subtracting.
stops.reflect: What is the one move that cleans up a fraction inside a fraction under a square root?

stages.desc: The Pythagorean identity, then the formula family: sum and difference, double-angle, half-angle, and power-reducing.

stops.title: Pythagorean identity: one value to another
stops.target: Use \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) to find \(\cos\theta\) from \(\sin\theta\) (or the reverse), then choose the sign from the quadrant.
stops.cold: If \(\sin\theta=-\tfrac{5}{13}\) and \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III, compute \(\cos\theta\).
stops.coldPlain: If sin(theta) = -5/13 and theta lies in Quadrant III, compute cos(theta).
stops.note: Show the identity, the square root, and how the quadrant picks the sign.
stops.solution: cos^2 = 1 - 25/169 = 144/169, so cos = plus or minus 12/13. In Quadrant III cosine is negative: -12/13.
stops.mistake: Stopping at +12/13 without checking the quadrant.
stops.again: If \(\sin\theta=\tfrac{7}{25}\) and \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II, compute \(\cos\theta\).
stops.reflect: The square root gives two answers. What decides which one you keep?

stops.title: Sum and difference formulas
stops.target: Find an exact value like \(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{12}\) by splitting into special angles and using a sum or difference formula.
stops.coldPlain: Find the exact value of cos(pi/12).
stops.note: Show which formula you chose and why, the special angles you split into, and the sign check from the quadrant.
stops.solution: pi/12 = pi/3 - pi/4. cos(a - b) = cos a cos b + sin a sin b = (1/2)(sqrt2/2) + (sqrt3/2)(sqrt2/2) = (sqrt2 + sqrt6)/4, about 0.9659.
stops.mistake: Writing cos(pi/3 - pi/4) = cos(pi/3) - cos(pi/4); cosine does not distribute.
stops.reflect: How do you remember which formula keeps the sign and which one flips it?

stops.title: Exact values in any quadrant
stops.target: For angles like \(\tfrac{17\pi}{12}\), split into special angles (one may be outside Quadrant I), substitute with signs, and check the sign of the answer.
stops.coldPlain: Find the exact value of cos(17pi/12).
stops.graphNote: It shows 17pi/12 drawn as 5pi/4 plus pi/6 on the unit circle.
stops.note: Show which formula you chose and why, the special angles you split into, and the sign check from the quadrant.
stops.solution: 17pi/12 = 15pi/12 + 2pi/12 = 5pi/4 + pi/6. cos(a + b) = cos a cos b - sin a sin b = (-sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) - (-sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt2 - sqrt6)/4, about -0.2588, negative as expected in Quadrant III.
stops.mistake: Dropping the negative signs of cos(5pi/4) and sin(5pi/4).
stops.again: Find the exact value of \(\sin\left(\tfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)\) and of \(\sin\left(-\tfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)\).
stops.reflect: How does the quadrant of the original angle give you a free check on your final answer?

stops.title: Double-angle formulas
stops.target: Given one trig value and the quadrant, find \(\sin 2\alpha\), \(\cos 2\alpha\), and \(\tan 2\alpha\).
stops.cold: If \(\sin\alpha=\tfrac35\) and \(\alpha\) is in Quadrant II, find \(\sin 2\alpha\), \(\cos 2\alpha\), and \(\tan 2\alpha\).
stops.coldPlain: If sin(alpha) = 3/5 and alpha is in Quadrant II, find sin(2 alpha), cos(2 alpha), and tan(2 alpha).
stops.note: Show how you found the missing trig value first and which double-angle formula you used.
stops.solution: First cos(alpha) = -4/5 (Quadrant II). sin 2a = 2 sin a cos a = -24/25. cos 2a = cos^2 a - sin^2 a = 16/25 - 9/25 = 7/25. tan 2a = -24/7.
stops.mistake: Computing sin(2 alpha) as 2 times 3/5 = 6/5, which is impossible for a sine.
stops.again: If \(\cos\beta=\tfrac{5}{13}\) and \(\beta\) is in Quadrant IV, find \(\sin 2\beta\) and \(\cos 2\beta\).
stops.reflect: Why do you need the cosine even when the problem only gives you the sine?

stops.title: Half-angle formulas
stops.target: Find exact values at angles like \(\tfrac{\pi}{8}\): ask "half of what?", use the half-angle formula, and take the sign from the quadrant of the half angle.
stops.coldPlain: Find the exact value of cos(pi/8).
stops.graphNote: It shows pi/8 as half of pi/4 on the unit circle.
stops.note: Show which formula you chose and why, the special angles you split into, and the sign check from the quadrant.
stops.solution: pi/8 is half of pi/4. cos(theta/2) = plus or minus sqrt((1 + cos theta)/2) with theta = pi/4. pi/8 is in Quadrant I, so plus: sqrt((1 + sqrt2/2)/2) = sqrt(2 + sqrt2)/2, about 0.9239.
stops.mistake: Using the quadrant of theta (the full angle) to choose the sign instead of the quadrant of theta/2.
stops.againA: Half of \(\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\); \(\tfrac{5\pi}{8}\) is in Quadrant II so sine is positive: \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}}{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}{2}\).[[graph:HALF2]]
stops.stretchA: Half of \(\tfrac{7\pi}{4}\), in Quadrant II, so cosine is negative: \(-\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{2}}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}{2}\).
stops.reflect: In the try-again, 5pi/4 is in Quadrant III but the answer is positive. Why?

stops.title: Power-reducing formulas
stops.target: Rewrite \(k\sin^2(nx)\) or \(k\cos^2(nx)\) with only first powers: \(\sin^2u=\tfrac{1-\cos 2u}{2}\), \(\cos^2u=\tfrac{1+\cos 2u}{2}\). The angle doubles.
stops.cold: Rewrite \(3\sin^2(4x)\) using only first powers of sine and cosine.
stops.coldPlain: Rewrite 3 sin^2(4x) using only first powers of sine and cosine.
stops.note: Show which power-reducing formula you used and how the angle changed.
stops.mistake: Keeping the angle as 4x instead of doubling it to 8x.
stops.stretch: Rewrite \(\sin^4 x\) using only first powers.
stops.reflect: Look at the graph: how do the midline 3/2 and the amplitude 3/2 show up in the rewritten form?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE1 CheckIt: an exact value, a value from a Pythagorean identity, and a power-reducing rewrite.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Find an exact value with a sum/difference or half-angle formula, use a Pythagorean identity with a quadrant, and power-reduce a squared trig function.
stops.cold:
(1) Find the exact value of \(\sin\left(\tfrac{11\pi}{12}\right)\).
(2) If \(\cos\theta=-\tfrac{8}{17}\) and \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II, compute \(\sin\theta\).
(3) Rewrite \(4\cos^2(5x)\) using only first powers of sine and cosine.
stops.coldPlain: (1) Find the exact value of sin(11pi/12). (2) If cos(theta) = -8/17 and theta lies in Quadrant II, compute sin(theta). (3) Rewrite 4cos^2(5x) using only first powers of sine and cosine.
stops.note: Show which formula you chose and why, the special angles you split into, and the sign check from the quadrant.
stops.solution: (1) 11pi/12 = 3pi/4 + pi/6; sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b = (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) + (-sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4, positive as expected in Quadrant II. (2) sin = +sqrt(1 - 64/289) = 15/17 (Quadrant II, sine positive). (3) 4(1 + cos 10x)/2 = 2 + 2cos(10x).
stops.mistake: In (1), using sin(3pi/4) = -sqrt2/2; sine is positive in Quadrant II.
stops.again: (1) Find the exact value of \(\cos\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{8}\right)\). (2) If \(\sin\theta=-\tfrac{20}{29}\) and \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV, compute \(\cos\theta\). (3) Rewrite \(2\sin^2(3x)\) using only first powers.
stops.againA: (1) Half of \(\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\), Quadrant II so negative: \(-\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}}{2}}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}}{2}\). (2) \(\tfrac{21}{29}\). (3) \(1-\cos(6x)\).
stops.reflect: Which formula family still feels shaky: sum/difference, half-angle, or power-reducing?
